c:borrow_loaned_message.why: RFC-0010's zero-copy path. rcl/rclcpp borrow a TYPED message the middleware owns (`LoanedMessage<T>`, `borrow_loaned_message`, `publish_loaned_message`, `return_loaned_message_from_publisher`); ours is a TOKEN over a byte range (`loan`/`commit`/`discard` on the publisher, `borrow`/`release` on the subscription) because C has no templates and the wrapper would need an allocator to own. NOTE the verbs differ as well as the shape, and only the shape has a reason -- W5 should decide whether `loan`/`commit`/`discard` should read `borrow_loaned_message`/`publish_loaned_message`/`return_loaned_message`.

c:event_publisher_count_cb_t.why: QoS events. rclcpp routes every event through one `set_on_new_qos_event_callback` plus a `QOSEventHandler` waitable the executor polls; ours are named callbacks per event (`on_liveliness_lost`, `on_offered_deadline_missed`, `on_message_lost`) registered on the entity. Constraint: no allocator for a per-event handler object and no wait-set to poll it from -- the callback is a fn-ptr in the entity's own static storage. The set of events is the same. This one reports matched-subscription count changes, which rclcpp answers by POLLING `get_subscription_count` -- see that row.

c:executor_add_subscription_in_group.why: adds a subscription to a named callback group, which rclc has no concept of (rclcpp does -- see `cpp:Node::create_callback_group` in the exec stage). Needed because RFC-0002 maps groups onto RTOS priority tiers.

c:executor_add_subscription_raw_with_inf.why: the raw + message-info form; see `c:publish_raw` and `rust:RawMessageInfo`.

c:executor_get_publishers_info_by_topic.why: phase-381 W3/W4. Same verb as ROS 2; the RECEIVER differs. ROS 2 hangs the graph off a node because each Node/Context owns a participant; a nano-ros image opens ONE session for the whole image -- a session per node is RAM a 128 KiB target does not have -- and the Executor owns it. NOT a `rename`: the name follows the receiver, and the receiver is where the session is. The endpoint carries no QoS. The GRANTED profile is what answers 'why is nothing arriving', no backend can read one back yet, and reporting the remote's DECLARED profile would be a confident wrong answer -- so the field is absent here and the rmw ABI's `*_UNKNOWN` sentinels carry it at the vtable seam, which is that ABI's documented way to say 'could not determine'.

c:get_zero_initialized_publisher.why: rcl's free-function spelling; ours is `nros_publisher_get_zero_initialized`, a method-style name on the type. See `c:get_zero_initialized_node`.

c:get_zero_initialized_subscription_cont.why: content-filtered topics are a DDS feature: the subscriber ships an SQL-ish expression the WRITER evaluates. Only one of our backends is DDS, and the filter would have to be a no-op on zenoh and XRCE -- a QoS-shaped promise two of three transports cannot keep. c:publish.why:
CORRECTED 2026-08-26 (phase-379 W5), re-verdicted rename -> divergence. The previous text argued from `nros_publisher_publish`, a symbol that has never existed: the only occurrence of that spelling anywhere in the tree is a comment in `examples/native/c/custom-transport-loopback/src/main.c` recording that phase 212 replaced the never-defined name. Our C publish entry points are `nros_publish_raw(publisher, data, len)` for the byte form and the codegen'd per-message `<pkg>_<msg>_publish(publisher, msg)` for the typed form (`packs/c/message.h.jinja`, e.g. `std_msgs_msg_int32_publish`). BOTH already have rcl's shape -- a free function taking the publisher first -- so there is no free-function-vs-method rename here. The cited precedent does not apply either, twice over: `c:get_zero_initialized_publisher` is verdict DECLINED, i.e. it argues for KEEPING our spelling, and it declines because ours there IS method-style, which ours here is not.
What actually differs is the SHAPE, and a platform constraint is why. `rcl_publish(publisher, ros_message, allocation)` is ONE type-erased function over a `const void *` ROS message plus an `rmw_publisher_allocation_t *`. We have no runtime typesupport dispatch and no allocator, so the typed publish is generated per message type (concrete struct pointer, no typesupport lookup, serializes into a `NROS_PUB_BUFFER_SIZE` stack buffer) and the type-erased publish is byte-oriented. The generated typed helper lives in a message header, which the report drops as message plumbing -- that, not an absence, is why this row reads theirs-only.
The `_raw` suffix on the byte form is a separate and still-open question, tracked by the SERIALIZED -> RAW pair (`c:take_serialized_message`, `c:publish_serialized_message`). It is not this row's.

rename.resolution: Not a rename. The word and the free-function shape already match; the row's premise (nros_publisher_publish) was a symbol that does not exist. Re-verdicted to divergence, naming the two real differences and their constraints: no `rmw_publisher_allocation_t` (no allocator) and per-type codegen instead of a `const void *` (no runtime typesupport dispatch). No code change; no target name invented.

c:publish_raw.why: the ours-only half of the SERIALIZED -> RAW rename pair (`c:take_serialized_message`).

c:publish_serialized_message.why: ROS 2 says SERIALIZED for the pre-CDR byte form; ours is `nros_publish_raw`. This row became the SOLE owner of that decision on 2026-09-03: the receive half (`c:take_serialized_message`) landed with phase-379 W6 decision 1, which renamed `try_recv_raw` -> `take_serialized`, so publish is the only side still saying RAW. One word, used consistently on both sides, and ours is the one that has to move. (Symbol spelling corrected 2026-08-26 (phase-379 W5): this row said `nros_cpp_publisher_publish_raw`; the C++ FFI symbol is `nros_cpp_publish_raw`.)

rename.resolution:
Target settled 2026-09-03 alongside the RECEIVE half, which did land: `nros_subscription_take_serialized` (`nros_generated.h:6459`) with `try_recv_raw` surviving as a `NROS_DEPRECATED_MSG` forwarder. This is the transmit half, unexecuted.

The `nros_`/`rcl_` prefix is NOT the difference — `normalize()` strips both symmetrically, so the keys reduce to `publish_raw` vs `publish_serialized_message`; `_message` and the module prefix stay dropped per `c:take_serialized_message`'s declined precedent.

Scope is wider than this C row implies: three ours-only halves are already rowed (`c:publish_raw`, `cpp:Publisher::publish_raw`, `rust:Publisher::publish_raw`), plus the `nros_cpp_publish_raw` FFI symbol and the C message template, which emits `return nros_publish_raw(...)` in generated code. Confirm the exact target symbol before executing — the row names the word `serialized` but never the symbol.

c:publisher_get_actual_qos.why: reports the QoS an entity actually ended up with, which can differ from what its call site requested. RE-VERDICTED 2026-09-04 (phase-417), declined -> gap, and the old justification DELETED rather than patched. It said QoS is selected at COMPILE time, so actual and requested are the same value by construction and an accessor would return its own input. That is false in both languages. QoS is a RUNTIME argument here (`nros_publisher_init_with_options(..., const struct nros_qos_t *qos, ...)`; `Node::create_publisher<M>(out, topic, qos)`), and a launch-lowered override table changes it AFTER the call site: `nros_node_set_qos_overrides` (`nros_generated.h:5205`) and `Node::set_qos_overrides` (`packages/api/nros-cpp/include/nros/node.hpp:292`) install `nros_qos_override_t` / `nros_cpp_qos_override_t` rows, and every entity created afterwards folds the matching `(topic, role)` entries in before the backend-compat check (`apply_qos_overrides`, `packages/api/nros-cpp/src/lib.rs:1283`, `packages/api/nros-c/src/qos.rs:194`). Actual differs from requested exactly when a deploy plan says so -- which is the accessor's whole use case. Nobody has built the readback: the folded profile is handed to the backend and not retained for a getter. That is a gap, not a decline.

c:publisher_get_context.why: reaches the context a publisher was created on. There is no separate context object -- see the init stage's `c:context_*`.

c:publisher_get_options.why: reads back the options a publisher was created with. `nros_publisher_options_t` ships (`nros_generated.h:2467-2474`) and `nros_publisher_init_with_options` takes it; what is missing is the READBACK -- nothing retains the struct on the handle and no `*_get_options` exists anywhere in our C surface, for any entity. CORRECTED 2026-09-04 (phase-417): this row said there is no runtime options struct. Seven ship and the correlator buckets all fourteen items `same` -- `nros_{node,publisher,subscription,service,client,action_client,action_server}_options_t` (`packages/api/nros-c/include/nros/nros_generated.h:1461,1729,2011,2474,2537,2556,2592`) plus a `*_get_default_options` for each, and `nros_node_options_t::domain_id_override` is a RUNTIME per-node domain. What is genuinely absent is the LIFECYCLE around one: no `*_options_copy`, no `*_options_fini`, and no `*_get_options` readback anywhere in the C surface.

c:publisher_get_rmw_handle.why: hands out the underlying rmw/rcl handle so a caller can bypass the API. Our RMW seam is the vtable in `nros/rmw_vtable.h` (RFC-0035) and is deliberately not reachable from an entity; see `c:node_get_rmw_handle`.

c:publisher_get_subscription_count.why: how many subscriptions are matched, RIGHT NOW. We notify on change (`nros_event_publisher_count_cb_t` + `nros_count_status_t`) and never let a caller ask, so code that wants to skip work when nobody is listening has to keep its own mirror of the callback's last value. Both forms are useful and rclcpp ships both. Phase 379 W3.

c:take.why:
RE-VERDICTED 2026-09-03 (phase-379 W6 decision 1), rename -> divergence: the WORD moved and what is left has a constraint behind it.
EXECUTED: `try_recv` -> `take` across C, C++ and Rust. Note the direction this went -- our own RMW vtable (`nros/rmw_vtable.h`) has spelled these slots `take` / `take_request` / `take_response` / `take_sequence` since phase-376 W3.b, so the USER API was the only layer still saying `try_recv`; the rename moves it onto the vocabulary the layer beneath it already used, which is also rcl's (`rcl_take`) and rclcpp's (`Subscription::take`). The contract collision that blocked this row is gone too: `PollingSubscription<M>::take(M&)` -- non-consuming, retained-latest, the opposite contract under the same word -- was DELETED, its `take_data()` / `take_new_data()` autoware mirrors (issue 0278) retained. Old C spellings survive as NROS_DEPRECATED_MSG `static inline` forwarders in `nros/subscription.h`, `nros/service.h` and `nros/client.h`; C++ as `[[deprecated]]` methods; Rust took a clean break with no shim, because a rename there breaks IMPLEMENTORS of the RMW traits rather than callers and a compile error is what a backend author wants.

That is exactly `c:publish`'s divergence mirrored on the receive side. The `nros_subscription_` prefix is not a second difference: it is a module prefix of the construction rcl itself uses (`rcl_client_fini`), and the precedent chain (`c:get_zero_initialized_publisher`, verdict DECLINED) argues for keeping ours.

rename.resolution: Executed 2026-09-03. `try_recv{,_raw,_sequence,_validated}` -> `take{,_serialized,_sequence,_validated}` in C, C++ and Rust; `try_recv_request` -> `take_request`, `try_recv_reply_raw` -> `take_response_raw`. The blocking contract collision was resolved by DELETING `PollingSubscription<M>::take(M&)` (a convenience duplicating `take_data()`, zero real callers) rather than by picking a third word. rust:PublishLoan.why: the publish-side loan: reserve the outgoing buffer, fill it in place, then `commit` (or `discard`). rclcpp's `borrow_loaned_message` is the same idea and rclrs has no equivalent at all. Ours differs in what backs the slot, which is the platform part: with no allocator the default backing is the publisher's own inline `[u8; TX_BUF]` and commit memcpys into the backend's outbound buffer, while `rmw-lending` swaps it for storage the backend owns (zenoh-pico's `z_bytes_from_static_buf`, XRCE's `ucdrBuffer` reservation) for a true zero-copy publish. `#[must_use]` because dropping without committing silently rolls the message back -- there is no destructor that can publish for you. See the pubsub stage's loan rows.

rust:Publisher.why: rclrs 0.5 splits every entity into `X` (an `Arc<XState>` alias) and `XState` (the inherent impl); ours is one type. The correlator folds the suffix, so the members listed here are the ones with no counterpart at all -- see `rust:PublisherState::get_subscription_count` and the loan rows.

rust:Publisher::assert_liveliness.why: manual liveliness assertion. rclcpp has `PublisherBase::assert_liveliness`, which folds onto ours by the *Base rule; recorded here because the Rust side has no rclrs counterpart -- rclrs does not expose liveliness at all.

rust:Publisher::buffer_error.why: constructs the error for a too-small serialisation buffer -- part of the caller-supplied-buffer contract in `rust:Publisher::publish`. rclrs owns the buffer and cannot fail this way.

rust:Publisher::notify_on_subscriber_rea.why: rclrs's async wait for the first matched subscription. Needs a future and a runtime to await it; the event form is `register_event_callback` (see the QoS-event rows).

rust:Publisher::publish.why: ours is `publish(&self, msg: &M, buf: &mut [u8])`; rclrs takes the message by value and serialises into a buffer it owns. The caller supplies the serialisation buffer because there is no allocator, and it is `&M` rather than `M` because a no_std caller usually wants to keep the message. This is the `no-allocator` constraint at the hottest call in the API.

rust:Publisher::publish_raw.why: the ours-only half of the SERIALIZED -> RAW rename pair (`c:take_serialized_message`).

rust:Publisher::publish_raw_with_attachm.why: see `cpp:Subscription::take_serialized_with_attachment` (this pointed at `cpp:Subscription::try_recv_raw_with_attachment`, which is now only the deprecated forwarder's row -- corrected 2026-09-04, phase-417).

rust:Publisher::register_event_callback.why: QoS events. rclcpp routes every event through one `set_on_new_qos_event_callback` plus a `QOSEventHandler` waitable the executor polls; ours are named callbacks per event (`on_liveliness_lost`, `on_offered_deadline_missed`, `on_message_lost`) registered on the entity. Constraint: no allocator for a per-event handler object and no wait-set to poll it from -- the callback is a fn-ptr in the entity's own static storage. The set of events is the same.

rust:Publisher::supports_event.why: asks whether the linked backend raises a given QoS event, because they differ: zenoh-pico raises no deadline events and Cyclone does. rclcpp assumes DDS and always claims support.

rust:Publisher::topic_name.why: reads back the topic a publisher was created on. C and C++ have it (`nros_publisher_get_topic_name`, `Publisher::get_topic_name`); the Rust publisher does not, so the three languages disagree with each other as well as with ROS 2. Phase 379 W3.

rust:Publisher::unsupported_event_error.why: the error `supports_event` predicts; see that row.

rust:PublisherHandle.why: the backend-agnostic publisher a component holds. rclrs's `Publisher` IS the rcl handle; ours is an index into the executor's static entity table, because the entity outlives the borrow that created it.

rust:ReadOnlyLoanedMessage.why: RFC-0010's zero-copy path. rcl/rclcpp borrow a TYPED message the middleware owns (`LoanedMessage<T>`, `borrow_loaned_message`, `publish_loaned_message`, `return_loaned_message_from_publisher`); ours is a TOKEN over a byte range (`loan`/`commit`/`discard` on the publisher, `borrow`/`release` on the subscription) because C has no templates and the wrapper would need an allocator to own. NOTE the verbs differ as well as the shape, and only the shape has a reason -- W5 should decide whether `loan`/`commit`/`discard` should read `borrow_loaned_message`/`publish_loaned_message`/`return_loaned_message`. rclrs splits read-only from writable loans by type; ours is one borrow with a const view.

rust:RecvView.why: the read side: a `!Send + !Sync` borrow of a subscription's receive buffer, so a callback reads the bytes without a copy and the drop releases the backend's lock. Same two backings as `rust:PublishLoan`. `!Send` is load-bearing rather than conservative -- the view aliases storage the next message will overwrite, and there is no allocator to move it into.

rust:Subscription::take.why: phase-379 W3. A POLLING receive, which rclrs has no public counterpart for: its subscription API is callback/worker-driven and its `take_*` methods are private (`fn take_response`, `fn take_feedback` in 0.7.0 — no `pub`). So this is ours-only against the RUST reference by construction, not by a naming choice. The NAME follows rcl (`rcl_take`) and rclcpp (`Subscription::take`), which do spell the non-blocking receive that way, and matches our own C surface. It was `try_recv` — Rust channel vocabulary that reads as a different contract to a ROS 2 user, when both forms are non-blocking and both report emptiness without failing. Renamed as a clean break, no deprecation shim: a shim would let call sites keep compiling against the old name silently, and five separate call sites were found only because the break made them hard errors.

Ours is a stack buffer whose capacity is a compile-time constant, which is the whole reason the knob exists: no allocator. Arrived on main between phase-379 W6's decision and its execution, so it carries the W6 verb (`take_*`, not `try_recv_*`) and a deprecated forwarder retired with the rest in W7 step 4.

cpp:NodeOptions::parameter_event_publish.why: phase-417 stage 0 — visible only because `rclcpp_compat.hpp` is now a translation unit (issue 1020). The shim ships this TYPE as a name, so its members stop inheriting "we do not have this type" and become their own claim. Not a new gap: a gap INSIDE a type we ship is a different statement from one about a type we do not. These specific ones are REFUSED LOUDLY (RFC-0087 W3.f): each stored its argument in a private field that nothing read and returned `*this`, so the idiomatic chained call compiled and configured nothing. They are `= delete` overloads now, sharing one diagnostic -- a refusal is per-CONCEPT, not per-symbol.
